title: A Sneeze Flies 8 Meters, So Why Do Your Eyes Shut? 🤧
description:
Why do your eyes close when you sneeze, and would your eyeballs really pop out if they stayed open? The sneeze reflex runs from your brainstem and fires a whole chain of muscles at once, eyelids included, while the sneeze cloud itself can drift about 8 meters (26 feet).

topic: Why do you sneeze with your eyes shut?
script: Your eyes slam shut every time you sneeze, and you almost can't stop it. Why? People say your eyeballs would pop out if they stayed open. That's a myth. The pressure builds in your chest, not behind your eyes. So what's going on? A tickle inside your nose sends a nerve signal to your brainstem, your sneeze control center. It doesn't ask permission. It fires a chain of muscles all at once. Deep breath in, chest squeezes, throat snaps open, and your eyelids get dragged along for the ride. Then the blast. A sneeze cloud can drift about eight meters. That's twenty-six feet! Some scientists think shut eyes help keep the spray out. A few people can sneeze with their eyes open, and their eyes stay right where they are. So next time you sneeze, will yours stay shut?
key_facts: The sneeze reflex is coordinated by the brainstem and fires many muscles at once; eyelid closure is part of that reflex
Eyeballs popping out if you sneeze with eyes open is a myth; the pressure builds in the chest and airways, not behind the eyes
A sneeze's turbulent cloud can travel about 7-8 meters (26 feet) (Bourouiba, MIT, JAMA 2020)
Some people can sneeze with their eyes open without harm
Some think closed eyes may help keep irritants or spray out (hedged)
